BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF NEVADA

Application of SV RNO Property Owner 1 LLC, under
the provisions of the Utility Environmental Protection
Act, for a permit to construct the South Valley
Temporary Power Generation Facility consisting of a
temporary 144 MW natural gas-fueled electric
generating facility and associated facilities to be located
on private land in Storey County, Nevada.

Docket No. 26-04026

Application of PR RNO Property Owner 1, LLC, under
the provisions of the Utility Environmental Protection
Act, for a permit to construct the Peru Ridge Self-
Generation Project consisting of a temporary 218 MW
natural gas-fueled electric generating facility and
associated facilities to be located on private land in
Storey County, Nevada.

Docket No. 26-04027

NTS SSS OS SS OS OOS OS OS

PROCEDURAL ORDER NO. 2

The presiding officer in this docket makes the following findings and conclusions:

1. On April 20, 2026, SV RNO Property Owner 1 LLC (“SV RNO”), filed with the
Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) an application, designated as Docket
No. 26-04026, under the provisions of the Utility Environmental Protection Act, for a permit to
construct the South Valley Temporary Power Generation Facility consisting of a temporary 144
megawatt natural gas-fueled electric generating facility and associated facilities to be located on
private land in Storey County, Nevada. SV RNO filed the application pursuant to the Nevada
Revised Statutes (“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code (“NAC”), Chapters 703 and 704,
including, but not limited to, NRS 704.820 through 704.900 and NAC 703.415 through 703.427.

2. On April 24, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Application for Utility
Environmental Protection Act Permit to Construct a Utility Facility in Docket No. 26-04026 and

SV RNO filed an amendment to the application.

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 Page 2

3. On April 20, 2026, PR RNO Property Owner 1, LLC (“PR RNO” and jointly with
SV RNO, the “Applicant”) filed with the Commission an application, designated as Docket No.
26-04027, under the provisions of the Utility Environmental Protection Act, for a permit to
construct the Peru Ridge Self-Generation Project consisting of a temporary 218 megawatt natural
gas fueled electric generating facility and associated facilities to be located on private land in
Storey County, Nevada. PR RNO filed the application pursuant to the NRS and the NAC,
Chapters 703 and 704, including, but not limited to, NRS 704.820 through 704.900 and NAC
703.415 through 703.427.

4. On April 24, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Application for Utility
Environmental Protection Act Permit to Construct a Utility Facility in Docket No. 26-04027 and
PR RNO filed an amendment to the application.

5. The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a
matter of right pursuant to NRS 703.301.

6. On May 20, 2026, Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy (“NCARE”)
filed notices of intent to be a party in both Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027.

7. On May 22, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Prehearing Conference in

Docket No. 26-04026.

8. On May 28, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Prehearing Conference in
Docket No. 26-04027.

9. On June 8, 2026, Applicant filed motions to dispense with the hearing in both
Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 (“Applicant Motions”).

10. On/June 12, 2026, NCARE filed responses in opposition to the motions in both

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 (“NCARE Opposition”).

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 Page 3

11. OnJune 15, 2026, Staff filed letters indicating it was not taking a position on the
pending motions in both Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027. On the same day, the presiding
officer held a prehearing conference in Docket No. 26-04026, attended by the Applicant, Staff
and NCARE, wherein consolidation, the pending motion and a procedural schedule were
discussed. No party objected to consolidation.

12. On/June 16, 2026, the presiding officer held a prehearing conference in Docket
No. 26-04027, attended by the Applicant, Staff and NCARE, wherein consolidation, the pending
motion and a procedural schedule were discussed. No party objected to consolidation.

13. On June 17, 2026, the Commission issued Procedural Order No. 1, consolidating
Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 for hearing purposes and setting a procedural schedule.

14. On June 22, 2026, the Applicant filed prepared direct testimony, and a reply to the
NCARE Opposition (“Applicant Reply”).

15. On July 1, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Hearing.

A, Motion
Applicant’s Position!

16. Applicant states that NRS 704.880 reflects a legislative judgment that an
uncontested application for a permit to construct can be decided without a hearing, providing that
“[t]he Commission, in its discretion, may dispense with the hearing on the application if, upon
the expiration of the time fixed in the notice thereof, no protest against the granting of the permit
has been filed by or in behalf of any interested party.” (Applicant Motions at 2.)

17. Applicant states that the time fixed in the Commission’s notice has expired, and

| As the Applicant Motions filed in Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 are almost identical, and the NCARE
Opposition and Applicant Reply are identical, the Commission, herein, will refer to the motion originally filed in
Docket No. 24-04026 for citation purposes.

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 Page 4

no protest against the granting of the permit has been filed, as Applicant contends that NCARE’s
notice of intent to intervene does not count as a protest. (/d.)

18. Applicant states that a notice of intent confers party status but does not register
opposition to the granting of the permit and is not a protest. Applicant further states that NRS
704.880 conditions the Commission’s discretion on whether a protest has been filed, not on
whether the docket has acquired parties. Applicant states that, should NCARE wish to be heard,
it may file a statement of its position and participate in the Commission’s consideration of the
written record without an evidentiary hearing. (/d. at 3.)

19. Applicant further states that the applications satisfy every UEPA filing, notice,
and service requirement, and that no disputed issue of material fact requires a hearing. Applicant
contends that the broader policy debate about data center load and behind-the-meter generation is
not before the Commission in these Dockets. (/d. at 3-5.)

NCARE Opposition

20. NCARE states that it is a proper party to the contested permit proceedings in the
above-captioned dockets pursuant to the Nevada Administrative Procedures Act (“APA”), which
governs and provides the minimum procedural requirements for adjudicatory proceedings before
state executive agencies. NCARE further states that, as a party to these contested cases, it has
the right to present relevant evidence and to examine and cross-examine witnesses at a hearing.
(NCARE Opposition at 3.)

21. NCARE states that Applicant’s position is incorrect and elevates form over
substance, contrary to the plain meaning of NRS 704.880. NCARE further states that, if
adopted, Applicant’s position would violate the minimum procedural requirements governing

adjudicatory proceedings before state executive agencies. NCARE states that the evidentiary

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 Page 5

process in this case is not concluded but is only beginning, and that it will actively pursue its
interests in this matter. (/d.)

22. NCARE asserts it has a right to hearings in both dockets, as the APA provides
that “[i]n a contested case, all parties must be afforded an opportunity for hearing after
reasonable notice,” and that an “[o]pportunity must be afforded all parties to respond and present
evidence and argument on all issues involved.” (/d. at 5, citing NRS 233B.121.)

23. | NCARE states that it opposes the applications as filed and will address the
required findings the Commission must make under NRS 704.890(1), and will examine and
cross-examine witnesses at hearing. (/d. at 12-13.)

Applicant’s Reply Position

24. Applicant states that UEPA establishes a distinct and streamlined statutory
framework, reflecting a legislative intent to resolve permit applications efficiently upon Staff and
Commission review of a completed application, consistent with statutory and regulatory
requirements and without unnecessary duplication. Applicant further states that the plain
language of NRS 704.880 vests the Commission with broad discretion to dispense with a hearing
absent the filing of a qualifying protest, and that NCARE’s filings do not satisfy that statutory
standard. Applicant states that, even if the Commission were to look beyond the threshold
statutory issue, NCARE has not identified any specific, material dispute of fact that would
necessitate an evidentiary hearing, particularly in light of the Legislature’s directive that prior
environmental findings be incorporated rather than re-litigated. (Applicant Reply at 2.)

25. Applicant states that NCARE’s Notice of Intent does not set forth substantive
objections to the application, identify disputed issues of material fact, or request that the

Commission deny or condition the permit in any particular manner, and it, therefore, cannot

Docket Nos. 26-04026 and 26-04027 Page 6

reasonably be construed as a protest within the meaning of NRS 704.880. (/d. at 5.)

26. Applicant states that the purpose of an evidentiary hearing is to resolve disputed
issues of fact that cannot otherwise be adequately evaluated. Applicant further states that, where
no such disputes are identified, a hearing serves little purpose other than to delay the proceeding
and impose additional burdens on the parties and the Commission. (/d. at 6.)

27. Applicant states that NCARE may present its position on the pending application
through a briefing memorandum, just as Staff does. Applicant further states that this procedure
allows NCARE to convey its views to the Commission without the need for evidentiary
submissions or live testimony, and confirms that dispensing with a hearing leaves NCARE with
a full and adequate opportunity to participate. (/d. at 7.)

Commission Discussion and Findings

28. Applicant bases its motions on the assertion that, because NCARE’s Notice of
Intent to Intervene did not use the word “protest,” it does not create a controversy requiring a
hearing.

29. The record does not support the conclusion that NCARE intervened for any
purpose other than to oppose the applications. Elevating the absence of the word “protest” over
the substance of NCARE’s participation would deprive a party of the opportunity to present
evidence at hearing, and the Commission declines to do so.

30. Although the motions are framed as a means of promoting administrative
efficiency, requiring the parties and the Commission to address them has produced the opposite
result.

31. | The Commission finds that NCARE’s Notice of Intent to Intervene is akin to a

protest, and, pursuant to NAC 703.530, construes it as such.

BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF NEVADA

PRESENT: — Chair Hayley Williamson
Commissioner Tammy Cordova
Commissioner Randy J. Brown
Assistant Commission Secretary Trisha Osborne
ORDER
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) makes the following
findings of fact and conclusions of law:
1. INTRODUCTION
Flying Bull Internet, LLC d/b/a NOVOS FIBER (“NOVOS FIBER”) filed with the
Commission an application, designated as Docket No. 25-12018, to voluntarily discontinue
telecommunication service conducted under CPC 3110.
I. SUMMARY
The Commission grants the application and cancels CPC 3110.
Il. PROCEDURAL HISTORY
* On December 31, 2025, NOVOS FIBER filed the application pursuant to Nevada Revised
Statutes (“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code Chapters 703 and 704, including, but not
limited to, NRS 704.390.

* The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a matter of right
pursuant to NRS 703.301.

* On January 5, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Application to Discontinue
Telecommunication Service.

Docket No. 25-12018 Page 2

* On June 25, 2026, Staff filed a briefing memorandum (“Staffs Briefing Memorandum”).

* On June 30, 2026, the Commission voted to adopt the recommendations contained within
Staffs Briefing Memorandum.

IV. APPLICATION
NOVOS FIBER’s Request

1. NOVOS FIBER seeks to voluntarily discontinue telecommunications service
conducted under CPC 3110. (Application at 1.) NOVOS FIBER states that it has never operated
in Nevada and that it has no customers; therefore, there are no customers whose service would be
impacted by this cancellation. (/d.)
Staff's Position

2. Staff states that NOVOS FIBER is current on regulatory obligations and that no
customers in Nevada will be impacted by this cancellation. (Staff's Briefing Memorandum at 1.)
Staff recommends that the Commission issue an order granting NOVOS FIBER’s application
and cancelling CPC 3110. (/d.)
Commission Discussion and Findings

3. The Commission adopts the analysis and recommendations contained in Staffs
Briefing Memorandum. The Commission finds that no customers in Nevada will be harmed by
the discontinuance of telecommunication services. Accordingly, consistent with Staffs
recommendations, and pursuant to NRS 704.390, the Commission grants the application and
cancels CPC 3110.

Therefore, it is ordered:

1. The application of Flying Bull Internet, LLC d/b/a NOVOS FIBER, designated as

Docket No. 25-12018, is granted.

ORDER
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) makes the following
findings of fact and conclusions of law:
I. INTRODUCTION
On April 14, 2026, Tenaska Power Services Co. (“Tenaska”) filed with the Commission
an annual report, for Nevada Gold Mines, designated as Docket No. 26-04017, on compliance
with the renewable energy portfolio standard (“RPS”) for compliance year 2025.

I. SUMMARY

The Commission approves the annual report and finds that Tenaska has complied with
the RPS requirements for 2025 for Nevada Gold Mines.

Il. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

* On April 14, 2026, Tenaska filed the annual report pursuant to the Nevada Revised Statutes
(“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code (“NAC”) Chapters 703 and 704, including, but
not limited to, NRS 704.7825, NAC 704.8877, and NAC 704.8879; additionally, Tenaska
requests confidential treatment of certain information contained in its Annual Report pursuant to
NRS 703.190 and NAC 703.527 et seq.

* On April 20, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Electric Provider’s Annual Report on
Compliance with the Nevada Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard.

* The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a matter of right

Docket No. 26-04017 Page 2

pursuant to NRS 703.301.

* On June 26, 2026, Staff filed a briefing memorandum (“Staff Briefing Memo”).
IV. ANNUAL REPORT

Tenaska’s Position

1, Tenaska states it has complied with its portfolio standard for compliance year
2025, and requests that the Commission issue an order finding that (a) Tenaska has complied
with its portfolio standard requirements for compliance year 2025 and (b) Tenaska may carry
forward the amount of portfolio energy credits (“PECs”) associated with portfolio energy
systems and energy efficiency measures set forth on Line 6c of the annual report. (Annual Report
at 1.)

Staff's Position

2. Staff states that Tenaska is required to meet the RPS requirements that were set
forth in NRS 704.7821, and under the provisions of NRS 704.7821(1)@), the RPS requirement
for compliance year 2025 stands at 34 percent of total retail sales. (Staff Briefing Memo at 1.)

3. Staff states that Tenaska reports sales of 450,108 megawatt-hours (“MWh”) to
Nevada Gold Mines, accordingly, Tenaska is required to acquire, and ultimately retire, a total of
153,037 renewable energy PECs (34 percent) for the 2025 RPS for Nevada Gold Mines, and that
Tenaska states that Nevada Gold Mines will themselves retire the PECs in compliance of the
filing. (/d. at 2.)

4. Staff states that in the Order in Docket No. 25-04007, Tenaska’s 2024 Annual
Report, the Commission issued a directive requiring that Tenaska’s 2025 compliance year filing
include copies of invoices or other verification for each Nevada customer to support the claimed

MWh sales, and Tenaska provided this information as Attachment F to the annual report. (/d.)

Docket No. 26-04017 Page 3

5. Staff recommends a similar directive be issued in this docket, to which, to
complete the necessary verification of Tenaska’s RPS requirements, on behalf of Nevada Gold
Mines, for 2025. (Id.) Staff also recommends that the Commission issue a compliance item
mandating that Tenaska, on behalf of Nevada Gold Mines, file evidence of its PEC retirements
within 30 days of a final order in this docket, and that the evidence submitted for this compliance
shall include a summary of the certificate serial numbers retired. (/d.)

Commission Discussion and Findings

6. The Commission finds that it is in the public interest to accept Staff's
recommendations: to find that Tenaska has met its required compliance with the RPS for
compliance year 2025 for Nevada Gold Mines; to issue a compliance item that mandates that
Tenaska submit evidence for Nevada Gold Mines of its PEC retirements, as discussed herein,
within 30 days of the effective date of this order, including specific evidence of a summary of the
certificate serial numbers retired; and to issue a directive mandating that Tenaska provide
verification for each Nevada customer to support its claimed MWh sales with its 2026
compliance year filing, similar to what was filed in Attachment F of the Report.

THEREFORE, it is ORDERED:

1. The Annual Report filed by Tenaska Power Services Co., for Nevada Gold Mines,
designated as Docket No. 26-04017, is approved.

BEFORE THE PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION OF NEVADA

Petition of Rural Telephone Company for a waiver )
from the requirement to file a new request for money)
from the Nevada Universal Service Fund. ) Docket No. 26-05003
)

At a general session of the Public Utilities
Commission of Nevada, held at its offices
on June 30, 2026.
PRESENT: Chair Hayley Williamson
Commissioner Tammy Cordova
Commissioner Randy J. Brown
Assistant Commission Secretary Trisha Osborne
ORDER
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) makes the following
findings of fact and conclusions of law:
I. INTRODUCTION
On May 4, 2026, Rural Telephone Company (“Rural Telephone”) filed with the Public
Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) a petition, designated as Docket No. 26-05003,
requesting a waiver from the requirement to file a new request for money from the Nevada
Universal Service Fund (“NUSF’”).
I. SUMMARY
The Commission grants the petition.
Til. PROCEDURAL HISTORY
* On May 4, 2026, Rural Telephone filed the petition pursuant to the Nevada Revised Statutes
(“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code (“NAC”) Chapters 703 and 704, including, but
not limited to, NAC 704.680482 and NAC 703.540.
* On May 11, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Petition for Affirmative Relief.

* The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a matter of right
pursuant to NRS 703.301.

* On June 3, 2026, Staff filed comments recommending approval of Rural Telephone’s petition.

Docket No. 26-05003 Page 2

* On June 25, 2026, the Commission’s Office of General Counsel (“General Counsel”) filed a
briefing memorandum recommending the Commission grant Rural Telephone’s petition.

* On June 30, 2026, at a regularly scheduled agenda meeting, the Commission voted to adopt the
recommendations contained in General Counsel’s briefing memorandum.

IV. PETITION
Rural Telephone’s Position

1. Rural Telephone requests waiver from the requirement to file a new request for
money from the NUSF. (Pet. at 1.). Specifically, Rural Telephone seeks approval of a two-year
waiver to file a new request pursuant to NAC 704.68048 to establish its annual draw from the
NUSF while continuing to receive its annual NUSF draw of $268,484 for two years until 2029.
(d.)

2. Rural Telephone explains that its last rate case (Docket No. 21-06047), which was
resolved through a stipulation with Staff, resulted in Rural Telephone’s current level of funding
through 2026; however, absent the requested relief, it would be required to file a rate case in
2026 to determine NUSF support for 2027. (/d. at 4-5.)

3. Rural Telephone provides that pursuant to NAC 704.68048(2)(c), as a small-scale
provider of last resort that draws from the NUSF, Rural Telephone must file a new request for
money every five years in a general rate case. (/d. at 4.) However, NAC 704.680482 provides
that Rural Telephone may petition for waiver of not more than two years from the rate case filing
requirement provided it satisfies NAC 704.680482(3) and the Commission finds that, based upon
information detailed in NAC 704.680282(4), it is not collecting excess earnings. (/d.)

4. Rural Telephone submits that it provided the information required by NAC

704.680482(4), including a) its annual operating revenue, expenses, and rate base as of its most

Docket No. 26-05003 Page 3

recent annual report;! b) Rural Telephone did not make any specific adjustments in its last rate
case given that it was a “black box” stipulation; c) Rural Telephone’s Commission-approved
return on rate base is 9.25 percent using a return on equity of 10.18 percent”; and d) it received
federal universal support totaling $453,894 in 2024. (/d. at 6-7.)

5. Rural Telephone states that it utilized consultants to update its annual report to
reflect the final cost study that was submitted to the National Exchange Carrier Association,
which also captured final updates in Rural Telephone’s 2024 audited financial statements,
including provisions for taxes. (/d. at 7-8.) Rural Telephone provides that the updated numbers
demonstrate that Rural Telephone’s rate of return was 3.77 percent, with a return on common
equity of 3.68 percent, falling below the Commission-approved 9.25 percent rate of return using
areturn of equity of 10.18 percent approved in Docket No. 21-05047. (/d. at 8.)

6. Rural Telephone states that its senior accounting employee recently retired and
other changes have been made in senior management. (/d.) Rural Telephone explains that it
would be a financial and operational burden to file a rate case in 2026 or 2027 while adjusting to
its new personnel changes. (/d.) Moreover, Rural Telephone is not collecting excess earnings.
(d.). Given those circumstances, Rural Telephone provides that it would be in the public
interest to grant its petition. (/d.)

Staff's Position
7. Staff recommends that the Commission approve Rural Telephone’s request for a

two-year waiver. (Staff’s Comments at 4.) Staff states that Rural Telephone provided the

' Per its annual report filed in Docket No. 25-01005, Rural Telephone’s Nevada intrastate annual operating revenue
for 2024 was $734,679; its Nevada intrastate operating expenses were $623,450 after the application of the Interstate
USF Revenues in the amount of $453,894 as a reduction; and its Nevada intrastate rate base was $2,151,034. (Pet.,
Ex. 1.)

? Rural Telephone provides, based upon its annual report filed in 25-01005, it had a -7.10 percent rate of return with
a -7.86 percent return on common equity. (See Pet. at 7 and Exhibit 1.)

Docket No. 26-05003 Page 4

information required by NAC 704.880482(4) and agrees with the company that granting its
waiver would be in the public interest. (/d. at 3.)

8. Staff explains that the petition is in the public interest because the Commission,
including Staff and Rural Telephone, are currently engaged in an investigation and rulemaking
that may make the significant use of public resources required for a general rate case, and the
financial and operational burden of such a proceeding, unnecessary by the time Rural Telephone
is required to make a new NUSF request. (/d.) Moreover, Staff notes that Rural Telephone’s
petition relies on the underlying stipulation in Docket No. 21-06047 where the parties did not
agree on an Alternative America Cost Model allocation methodology and the construction of
NAC 704.680482(4)(d), issues which may be more efficiently resolved in the ongoing
investigation and rulemaking before parties are required to address them in a general rate case.
(Id. at 3-4.)

Commission Discussion and Findings

9. NAC 704.680482(1) provides a vehicle for telecommunications companies who
are small-scale providers of last resort to seek a two-year waiver of the filing of a general rate
case. NAC 704.680482(2) gives the Commission discretion to grant a limited, two-year waiver
to small scale providers of last resort provided that the company seeking waiver demonstrates
that granting of the waiver is 1) in the public interest; and 2;) upon examining the information
required by NAC 704.680482(4), the Commission determines that the company is not over-
earning. Here, Rural Telephone met the technical requirements of NAC 704.680482 and
demonstrated that such a waiver is in the public interest.

10. Specifically, the Commission finds that in Rural Telephone’s petition, it provided:

its most recent annual operating revenue, annual operating expenses and rate base as a small-

Docket No. 26-05003 Page 5

scale provider of last resort, based upon its most recent annual report at the time of filing;
detailed adjustments, or the lack thereof, made in its last general rate case; its current
Commission-approved return on equity and a calculation of what the company is actually
earning; and disclosed the total amount of federal universal support that Rural Telephone
received in 2024 in satisfaction of NAC 704.680482(4). Rural Telephone also provided updated
calculations of its return on equity made after the filing of its annual report to reflect the final
cost study that was submitted to the National Exchange Carrier Association.

11. The Commission finds that Rural Telephone’s most recent annual report filed
with the Commission, and an updated annual report provided with its petition, demonstrate that
Rural Telephone is earning a return on equity below their authorized level. Notably, Rural
Telephone’s current authorized rate of return is 9.25 percent. Based upon the figures contained
in its 2024 annual report, Rural Telephone operated with a rate of return of -7.10 percent. An
examination of updated numbers contained in a supplemental update produced by third-party
consultants placed that figure at 3.68 percent. However, even with updated numbers, Rural
Telephone is not exceeding its authorized rate of return, thus satisfying NAC 704.680482(3)(b).

12. The Commission finds and agrees with Rural Telephone and Staff that approval
of the instant petition would be in the public interest. More specifically, given Rural
Telephone’s transitional period with senior accounting employees, its lower earnings relative to
its authorized rate of return, and the pending investigation and rulemaking in Docket No. 24-
12030 that might reduce expenditures and burdens involved with rate case proceedings, a two-
year waiver would serve the public interest. Accordingly, the Commission grants the petition.

Therefore, it is ordered:

PRESENT: Chair Hayley Williamson
Commissioner Tammy Cordova

ORDER
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) makes the following
findings of fact and conclusions of law:
I. INTRODUCTION

On April 13, 2026, Switch Ltd. (“Switch”) filed with the Commission an annual report,
designated as Docket No. 26-04015, on compliance with the renewable energy portfolio standard
(“RPS”) for compliance year 2025 (the “Compliance Year”).

I. SUMMARY

The Commission approves the annual report and finds that Switch has complied with the
RPS requirements for 2025.

Ii. PROCEDURAL HISTORY

* On April 13, 2026, Switch filed the annual report pursuant to the Nevada Revised Statutes
(“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code (“NAC”) Chapters 703 and 704, including, but
not limited to, NRS 704.7825, NAC 704.8877, and NAC 704.8879, additionally, Switch requests
confidential treatment of certain information contained in its annual report pursuant to NRS
703.190 and NAC 703.527 et seq.

* On April 17, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Electric Provider’s Annual Report on
Compliance with the Nevada Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard.

* The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a matter of right
pursuant to NRS 703.301.

Docket No. 26-04015 Page 2

* On June 25, 2026, Staff filed a briefing memorandum (“Staff Briefing Memo”).
IV. ANNUAL REPORT
Switch’s Position

1, Switch states it is committed to being 100% green and meets the RPS statutory
requirement for the Compliance Year, and that based upon NV Energy’s monthly usage bills,
Switch’s Compliance Year Nevada load is 1,397,988 megawatt-hour (“MWh”), and Switch
retired sufficient portfolio energy credits (“PECs”)/renewable energy credits to meet 100% of its
load in this Compliance Year. (Annual Report at 1.)

Staff's Position

2. Staff states that Switch takes retail service from Tenaska Power Services Co.
(“Tenaska”) pursuant to NRS 704B, and Tenaska, therefore, is a “Provider of Electric Service”
as defined in NRS 704.7808 and must comply with the Nevada RPS set forth in NRS 704.78213,
but that on April 13, 2026, Tenaska filed its Annual Report (Docket No. 26-04014) which
acknowledges that Switch filed the present Annual Report to also demonstrate Tenaska's
compliance with its RPS requirements for the retail sales it made to Switch. (Staff Briefing
Memo at 1.)

3. Staff states that pursuant to the provisions of NRS 704.78213, Tenaska is required
to meet the RPS requirements that were set forth in NRS 704.7821, and under the provisions of
NRS 704.7821(1)(j), the RPS requirement for compliance year 2025 stands at 34 percent of total
retail sales. (/d. at 2.)

4. Staff states that for the Compliance Year, Switch’s total load was 1,397,988
MWh, accordingly, Switch is required to acquire and retire PECs equal to 475,316 MWh

(475,316,000 PECs) on behalf of its provider for the 2025 RPS. (/d.)

Docket No. 26-04015 Page 3

5. Staff states that Switch summarizes its portfolio credit position in Section II of its
Compliance Report, as Switch received 438,462,000 PECs in the Compliance Year from Switch
Station 1 and 2 pursuant to agreements under NV Energy’s Green Rider Program, and states that
it retired additional credits to cover its entire compliance year load of 1,397,988 MWh, and
Switch is not requesting to carry forward PECs on behalf of Tenaska at this time. (/d.)

6. Staff states that in previous dockets pertaining to Switch’s annual reports, the
Commission has issued orders containing directives for Switch to provide copies of monthly
invoices or other verification to support the claimed MWh sales from that compliance year
within the relevant compliance filing, and that Staff has found this compliance helpful, and
recommends a similar directive be issued in this docket for compliance year 2026. (/d.)

7. Staff states that information submitted by Switch on behalf of its provider
demonstrates that Tenaska is in compliance with the requirements of the RPS for the Compliance
Year for the retail sales made to Switch, and that Staff has verified that the Annual Report
contains the reporting information required by NAC 704.8879(2). (/d.)

Commission Discussion and Findings

8. The Commission finds that it is in the public interest to accept Staff's
recommendations: to find that Switch is facilitating Tenaska’s compliance with the RPS for the
Compliance Year by retiring a specified number of PECs for their respective retail sales to
Switch.

9. Additionally, the Commission will issue the directive requested by Staff.

///
//1

///

Docket No. 26-04015 Page 4

1. The Annual Report filed by Switch Ltd. on behalf of Tenaska Power Services Co.
designated as Docket No. 26-04015, is approved.

renewable portfolio standard for compliance year 2025 for its sales to Switch Ltd.

ORDER 
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada (“Commission”) makes the following 
findings of fact and conclusions of law: 
I.
INTRODUCTION 
On April 15, 2026, Shell Energy North America (US), L.P. (“Shell Energy”) filed with 
the Commission an annual report, designated as Docket No. 26-04019, on compliance with the 
renewable energy portfolio standard (“RPS”) for compliance year 2025. 
II.
SUMMARY 
The Commission approves the annual report and finds that Shell Energy has complied 
with the RPS requirements for 2025. 
III.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
• On April 15, 2026, Shell Energy filed the annual report pursuant to the Nevada Revised 
Statutes (“NRS”) and the Nevada Administrative Code (“NAC”) Chapters 703 and 704, 
including, but not limited to, NRS 704.7825, NAC 704.8877, and NAC 704.8879; additionally, 
Shell Energy requests confidential treatment of certain information contained in its Annual 
Report pursuant to NRS 703.190 and NAC 703.527 et seq. 
• On April 20, 2026, the Commission issued a Notice of Electric Provider’s Annual Report on 
Compliance with the Nevada Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard. 
• The Regulatory Operations Staff of the Commission (“Staff”) participates as a matter of right 
pursuant to NRS 703.301. 

Docket No. 26-04019 
Page 2 
• On June 25, 2026, Staff filed a briefing memorandum (“Staff Briefing Memo”). 
IV.
ANNUAL REPORT 
Shell Energy’s Position
1.
Shell Energy states that it had no sales of energy in Nevada in compliance year 
2025, and consequently, no RPS obligation; therefore, Shell Energy provides that it has retired 
sufficient portfolio energy credits (“PECs”) to meet its requirements for 2025. (Annual Report at 
1-2.). 
Staff’s Position 
2.
Staff states that Shell Energy had zero retail electricity sales in Nevada during 
compliance year 2025 and thus had zero RPS procurement requirement for compliance year 
2025. (Staff Briefing Memo at 1.) 
3.
Staff states that effective December 31, 2024, the contract under which Shell 
Energy supplied electric power to its only Nevada based customer, Nevada Gold Mines LLC 
(“NGM”), was terminated. Consequently, Shell Energy did not sell electricity to retail customers 
in the State of Nevada during compliance year 2025. (Id.) 
4.
Staff states that the information submitted by Shell Energy demonstrates that it 
complies with the requirements of the RPS for compliance year 2025, and Staff has verified that 
the Annual Report contains the reporting information required by NAС 704.8879(2). (Id. at 2) 
Commission Discussion and Findings 
5.
The Commission finds that it is in the public interest to accept Staff’s 
recommendations: to find that Shell Energy has met its required compliance with the RPS for 
compliance year 2025 as Shell Energy had no sales in Nevada in 2025, and therefore, no RPS 
requirement in Nevada for compliance year 2025.
